title: His father's spot jobs and the musicians' union building on Bourbon Street
summary: His father played trumpet taps at Italian society events, was vice president of Local 174 and engineered the cheap Depression purchase of the union home; a larger Elks building was turned down.

story.theme_name: The musicians' union: cards, locals, and the Black-white merger
story.community_name: The musicians' union: cards, scale and the black-white merger

blocks.x: Uh-huh. And, uh... The... And then, uh... He did play music... On the side. He played some spot jobs, you may... Would say. Uh... One... One thing I do remember... That he was... There was a couple of organizations... Fraternal organizations... Primarily Italian organizations... That, uh... They used to have... A trumpet player... Or bugler... To play the taps...

At the... At the... At the monument... Or the mausoleum... Where... Where they were buried on a... On an anniversary... Or an occasion of some sort. That was a habit in those days. And he would go out there... And play me... Maybe play that favorite song... Of the deceased... Or something like that. And, uh... He... He was, uh... Also, uh... Vice president of the local... 174. And he was on the board of directors... For many years. He was responsible... For buying... For... 1316... Or 13... Or something... Bourbon Street. They bought that... In the midst of... The 1930... Depression... Where homesteads... Were going broke... Where he managed to get... Enough money... To buy... Eight thousand dollars... I think for about... Three thousand dollars... He bought... Eight thousand dollars... Worth of stock... And bought the musicians union... Home for eight thousand dollars... On a... It was a... It was a manipulation... Of some sort... I don't remember...

That's where we were... Down there... On Bourbon Street... And, uh... He was responsible... He and Johnny Detroit... Well... There were... Two musicians... Who were more businessmen... Than the average musician... Because musicians are not... Not... Musicians are not businessmen... Uh-huh... In fact, my father had the opportunity... After we... After we bought that place down there... At a stupid price... Sam Burglass... On Burglass Furniture Store... On Canal Street... He was the... Exalted ruler... Of the... Elks... BPOE... And they had that building... Over there on... Elks Place... That, uh... They were willing to give away... For sixty thousand dollars... Yeah... And they offered it to the... Our union... And I said... Oh, it's too big for us... It's too big for us... Well... I don't know whether you know it... But that place is worth... About three million dollars today... Is that right? Wow... And, uh... It was just too big for us... Sixty thousand dollars... Yeah... So, uh... He knew how to manipulate things... He... He was a... He was a manipulator... He was not crooked... But he took advantages of situations... And he with other people... Were... right in the 100 block of, I think it was Bourbon Street. Or Royal Street. I think it was either Royal or Bourbon. But they were in a building right in there that they gave away for nothing. They're not businessmen, believe me, though.

Right around there. Right very close to there. It was on the lake side. Glucks was on the river side. But it was right in there. And he's been a, I don't know that he was a charter member of our local, but he was a member for many, many years. He was a member for a long time.
